records.our_prose: Okra companion pairings are largely traditional rather than trial-tested, and the useful ones fall into a few practical roles. As a tall, late, heat-loving Malvaceae, okra does not share the disease load of tomatoes and other nightshades, so it makes a good rotational and bed neighbor for them rather than a competitor for the same soil pests. Southern peas and other legumes are a long-standing Southern partner, fixing nitrogen and, in the case of cowpeas, acting as a trap that pulls stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs off the pods. Quick crops like lettuce and radish use the open ground while young okra is small, and flowering insectary plants draw the bees and beneficial insects that help. The firmest rule is a rotation one: keep okra away from cotton, hibiscus, and other mallows, which share its root-knot nematode and fusarium problems.

records.our_prose: Okra's main problems are sucking and chewing pests on the pods (aphids, corn earworm, stink bugs and leaf-footed bugs) and soilborne diseases (root-knot nematode, fusarium wilt, southern blight). Pitted or distorted pods point to stink bugs; sudden wilt with a rotted stem base is southern blight; stunting with knotted roots is root-knot nematode, which also opens the way for wilt.

records.our_prose: Okra needs only modest feeding, and too much nitrogen makes a big leafy plant with few pods. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the soil before planting, then give a light feeding once the first pods come in and again a few weeks later. Water it in, and keep the granules off the stems and leaves.

records.our_prose: Okra is a moderate, steady feeder over a long season, and the classic mistake is too much nitrogen, which gives a tall leafy plant with few pods. Work a complete fertilizer such as 10-10-10 into the bed before planting (about 2 pounds per 100 square feet), then side-dress lightly once the first pods are harvested and again two to three weeks later, with 10-10-10 or a nitrogen source like calcium nitrate. Pair feeding with steady moisture, since the nutrients only help a plant that is not also drought-stressed at pod set.

records.our_prose: Pick okra young and often. Pods are ready just a few days after the flower opens, when they are 2 to 4 inches long and still tender. Cut them off with a short stem rather than pulling. Check every day or two, because okra pods turn tough and stringy within a day or two if you leave them. A good test: a ready pod snaps easily and your thumbnail dents the tip; if it is hard, it is too old to eat. Pull off any pods that got too big and compost them, so the plant keeps making new ones. Many okra plants have little spines, so wear long sleeves and gloves when you pick.

records.our_prose: Try not to grow okra or its relatives (cotton, hibiscus) in the same spot more than once every 3 years or so. Moving it around the garden and following it with corn, grasses, or beans helps avoid a buildup of soil pests and disease. Clean up old stalks at the end of the season too.

records.source_context: Do not till bark or wood chip mulches into the soil close to plants, as they will tie up nitrogen as they decompose. Synthetic mulches should be removed and discarded at the end of the season or when they are no longer useful as mulches. Organic mulch materials can be turned into the soil with a spade or rototiller or placed in your compost pile.

records.our_prose: About 1 inch of water per week once established, more in extreme heat or on sandy soil. Okra is notably drought-tolerant for a vegetable thanks to a deep taproot, but it sets and sizes the most pods with steady moisture, so do not let it bake dry during flowering and pod set.

records.source_context: If the soil becomes too dry, their growth may be seriously limited. Most vegetable crops require 1 inch of water per week for optimum pro- duction. If your area does not receive this amount of rainfall each week during the growing season, you will need to irrigate your garden using overhead sprinklers, soaker hoses, drip tape or hand watering.
